records.place: Bolgheri, Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC, on the Tuscan coast

wine.name: Sassicaia
wine.classification: A DOC of its own since 2013, a sub-zone of Bolgheri DOC from 1994
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority and at least four fifths by rule, with Cabernet Franc for the rest.
wine.sites: Parcels of the estate between about 100 and 400 metres, facing west and south west, on the slopes below Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, where the Cabernet was planted in the 1940s, and lower down; soils of limestone, marl and pebbles with some clay, the stones that give the wine its name.
wine.making: Each variety is fermented apart in temperature controlled stainless steel and macerated for ten days to about two weeks; the malolactic conversion follows in steel. The wine then spends about two years in French barriques, a share of them new, where the rules ask at least eighteen months in barrels of no more than 225 litres.
wine.glass: Cassis and redcurrant with cedar, tobacco leaf and the Mediterranean scrub of the coast, more fragrance than weight; medium to full bodied, with fresh acidity and fine, close grained tannin.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first eight to ten years, it opens slowly and lasts for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The denomination of the estate's own vineyards, a sub-zone of Bolgheri until it became a DOC of its own in 2013.
The Italian protected appellation, with rules for the grapes, the yields and the time in barrel.
The Incisa della Rocchetta family's estate at Bolgheri, which makes the wine.

records.table: Sassicaia began the fame of the Tuscan coast: Tenuta San Guido's Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Cabernet Franc from stony slopes at Bolgheri, with a DOC of its own since 2013. Cedar and cassis ride on fine tannin; decant it young.
records.story: Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta (1899 to 1983) took the wines of Bordeaux as his model, and in 1944 he planted a small vineyard near Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, with Cabernet among its vines. By the estate's account the cuttings came from the Salviati family's estate near Pisa; the story that they came from Lafite is often told, and the family has denied it. Until 1967 the wine was made for family and friends alone, named Sassicaia, the stony place, for its ground. Persuaded by his son and his nephew of the Antinori family, he sold it from the 1968 vintage, released in the early 1970s as a Vino da Tavola, since no DOC then covered it. Giacomo Tachis (1933 to 2016), the Antinori oenologist, brought temperature controlled fermentation to the cellar, and in 1978 Sassicaia won a tasting of Cabernets from around the world held by Decanter in London. When the Bolgheri DOC first admitted red wine in 1994, Sassicaia became its named sub-zone, and in 2013 Bolgheri Sassicaia became a DOC of its own. Its 1985 is a vintage of history. Sassicaia tells the Super Tuscan story in one bottle: a private Cabernet, a table wine, then a denomination of its own.

others.name: Guidalberto
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, first released in the 2000s.

others.name: Le Difese
others.note: The third wine, Cabernet Sauvignon with Sangiovese, a lighter and earlier red of the house.

traps: Sassicaia is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc; Ornellaia is the Bolgheri red with Merlot and Petit Verdot in its blend.
The first vintage sold was 1968; the wines made before it were for the family and never sold.
Bolgheri Sassicaia became a DOC of its own in 2013; from 1994 it was a sub-zone of Bolgheri DOC, and before that a Vino da Tavola.

cards.front: Sassicaia: what does the name mean, and what in the vineyard gave it?
cards.back: The stony place: the pebbles and stones in the estate's soils of limestone and marl.

cards.front: With which vintage did Tenuta San Guido begin to sell Sassicaia?
cards.back: 1968, released in 1971; the wines made before it were kept for family and friends.

questions.q: Under the rules of Bolgheri Sassicaia and the house's own blend, which grapes make Sassicaia?
opts: Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Petit Verdot
questions.exp: The rules ask at least four fifths Cabernet Sauvignon, and the estate completes it with Cabernet Franc; Merlot and Petit Verdot belong to Ornellaia's blend, not to Sassicaia's.

questions.q: Bolgheri Sassicaia stopped being a sub-zone of Bolgheri and became a DOC of its own. In which year?
questions.exp: It became a denomination in its own right in 2013; 1994 is the year it became a named sub-zone, when the Bolgheri DOC first admitted red wine.

Consorzio Tutela Vini Bolgheri DOC: Bolgheri Sassicaia production code
Decanter: Wine Legend, Tenuta San Guido Sassicaia 1985

report: Primary: the estate's history page, its page on the denomination and its vintage sheets (2013 to 2022) for the making, read through search summaries, with the consorzio's English rules for Bolgheri Sassicaia (at least four fifths Cabernet Sauvignon, at least eighteen months in barriques of 225 litres, the name from the stones of the soil); the rest rests on FINE+RARE, Decanter, Wikipedia's Tenuta San Guido and Tachis pages, the Wine Scholar Guild and VinePair, each fact in two.

Mario Incisa della Rocchetta is now named with both dates, 1899 to 1983: the refuter found the birth year in Visit Tuscany and the Wein.plus glossary, with the estate's history page in the same search.
The vintage that won Decanter's tasting of 1978 is the 1972 on the estate's site, at FINE+RARE and Winerist, but the 1975 in Decanter's Wine Legend of the 1985, so the story gives no vintage.

The library's p-tenuta-san-guido and w-sassicaia call Sassicaia an IGT before its own denomination, which they date to 1994; the estate, the consorzio, the Wine Scholar Guild and VinePair say it was Vino da Tavola from 1968 until it became a sub-zone of Bolgheri DOC in 1994, and a DOC of its own only in 2013, which the record follows.
The library's claim that it is the only Italian DOC of a single estate is not repeated here; the record says only that the denomination is the estate's own.

Tachis's dates rest on Wikipedia and The Drinks Business notice of his death at 82 in February 2016, the second not listed for want of room; the Antinori nephew who persuaded the founder is Wikipedia's and FINE+RARE's account.

Guidalberto's first vintage was not confirmed, so the note keeps the library's words, the 2000s; the cuttings from the Salviati estate are the estate's own account, the Lafite story FINE+RARE's, told as a story.
Living, kept out: the founder's son and granddaughter, both already in people.json; Graziana Grassini, the estate's oenologist after Tachis in FINE+RARE's account, should join people.json.

changed: story: Mario Incisa della Rocchetta was "who died in 1983"; now "(1899 to 1983)", born in Rome in 1899 by Visit Tuscany and the Wein.plus glossary, with the estate's history in the same search.

story: the vineyard of 1944 was "a small vineyard of Cabernet"; now "with Cabernet among its vines", since the estate's history gives mixed first plantings and the selection of the Cabernets between 1960 and 1968.

story, traps and cards: "From 1945 to 1967" and "the wines of 1945 to 1967" cut, since no source read gives 1945 (one gives 1948 for the first wine); now the wines made before 1968 were kept for the family.
cards: the release was "in the early 1970s"; now "in 1971", the estate's own wines page.

story: Tachis "brought temperature controlled fermentation and French barriques"; now temperature controlled fermentation only, since the accounts date the French barriques to the 1977 vintage or keep Slavonian barriques until 1982.

wine.making: "each variety and parcel is fermented apart with its own yeasts" now "each variety is fermented apart", the sheets giving a wild ferment for 2020 alone among those read and no parcels; the maceration "about two weeks" now "ten days to about two weeks", as the 2015 sheet gives.
wine.making: the rule was "barrels of 225 litres"; now "barrels of no more than 225 litres", as the consorzio's production code says.

wine.sites: "from the first vineyard of 1944 near Castiglioncello di Bolgheri downwards" now "on the slopes below Castiglioncello di Bolgheri, where the Cabernet was planted in the 1940s, and lower down", the estate's denomination page.

sources: FINE+RARE, the denomination page and Wikipedia's Tachis replaced by the 2020 vintage sheet, the consorzio's production code and the Wein.plus glossary; the report line on the birth year rewritten.
open: The vintage that won the Decanter tasting of 1978 stays out: the 1972 in most accounts, the 1975 in one Decanter piece, and Decanter's 1978 vintage guide speaks of the 1978.
The birth year rests on two secondary sources and a search summary of the estate's history that a second search on the estate's domain did not repeat.
The library's only single estate DOC in Italy was not tested; the record keeps to the consorzio's words, production restricted to the estate.

wine.name: Ornellaia
wine.classification: Bolgheri DOC Superiore, the DOC's red with at least two years of ageing, one in oak
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon in the lead, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in shares that change with the year.
wine.sites: Parcels across the estate on the plain and lower slopes below Bolgheri, on soils the house calls marine, alluvial and volcanic in origin: sand and marl lower down, clay dotted with limestone pebbles a little higher.
wine.making: Each parcel and variety is fermented apart in stainless steel and, in later vintages, concrete tanks, and the malolactic conversion takes place mostly in barriques, most of them new. After about a year the lots are blended and returned to barrel for six to eight months more, eighteen to twenty months in all, and the wine then rests a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Ripe cassis, black plum and black cherry with graphite, sweet tobacco and sun warmed herbs; full bodied and polished, with ripe, dense tannin and a long, generous finish.
wine.ageing: Generous enough to drink at eight to ten years, it is fuller at fifteen, and a strong vintage keeps two decades or more.
wine.serve: A Bordeaux glass at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle takes an hour or two in a decanter, and an old one should be poured gently off its sediment.

label.means: The Bolgheri red aged at least two years from the January after the harvest, one of them in oak.
The estate at Bolgheri founded in 1981, where Masseto was first made.

records.table: Ornellaia leads with Cabernet Sauvignon, adding Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot: the Bolgheri Superiore of Tenuta dell'Ornellaia, founded in 1981 by a younger son of the Antinori family. Poured beside Sassicaia, it reads riper and fuller.
records.story: It was a younger son of the Antinori family, the Florentine wine house, who founded Tenuta dell'Ornellaia on land at Bolgheri in 1981; the founder of Sassicaia was his uncle by marriage. André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), a Russian born veteran of the Napa Valley, advised on the planting, and on his advice a hill of blue clay on the estate went to Merlot. The first Ornellaia was the 1985. The clay hill gave its first wine in 1986, bottled as Merlot dell'Ornellaia, and from the 1987 vintage it was called Masseto. Red wine entered the Bolgheri DOC, until then a denomination of white and rosé, in 1994, and Ornellaia carries its Superiore rank. From 1999 the Californian house of Robert Mondavi bought into the estate, with the Frescobaldi family of Florence soon beside it as partners, and in 2005, after Mondavi had itself been sold, the Frescobaldi bought the rest. Masseto was later run as an estate of its own. Ornellaia is the wine that showed Bolgheri was a region and not one estate, and the riper, Merlot inflected foil to Sassicaia's Cabernet with Cabernet Franc.

others.name: Le Serre Nuove dell'Ornellaia
others.note: The second wine, labelled Bolgheri DOC Rosso, from the same estate.

others.name: Masseto
others.note: Merlot from the blue clay hill of the estate, first made in 1986 and named Masseto from the 1987 vintage.

traps: Ornellaia is Bolgheri DOC Superiore, not Toscana IGT and not Bolgheri Sassicaia.
Masseto is a Merlot from the estate's clay hill, not the grand vin of Ornellaia, and it was later run as a separate estate.
Ornellaia was founded by a younger son of the Antinori family, not by Marchesi Antinori, the family's Florentine house.

cards.front: Ornellaia: how long after the estate's founding did the first vintage come, and which was it?
cards.back: 1985, four years after the estate was founded in 1981.

cards.front: Which Merlot began on a blue clay hill of Ornellaia, first bottled as Merlot dell'Ornellaia?
cards.back: Masseto, first made with the 1986 vintage and named so from the 1987.

questions.q: A guest compares Ornellaia with Sassicaia. Which grape does Ornellaia's blend use that Sassicaia's does not?
questions.exp: Ornellaia blends Merlot, with Petit Verdot, into Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc; Sassicaia is Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc, so Cabernet Franc is in both.

questions.q: Which family bought the whole of Tenuta dell'Ornellaia in 2005, after sharing it with a Californian house?
questions.exp: The Frescobaldi, partners beside Robert Mondavi from the early 2000s, bought the rest in 2005; a younger Antinori son had founded the estate in 1981 and sold it on.

sources.title: Ornellaia: Ornellaia 2022, Bolgheri DOC Superiore Rosso, technical sheet
Decanter: The making of a megastar, Masseto

report: Primary: the estate's history page (founded 1981, first wine 1985), its terroir page (soils) and its technical sheets of 2022 and 2016 (steel and concrete, malolactic mostly in barrel, about seven tenths new, about eighteen to twenty months, a year in bottle), read through search summaries; the Mondavi and Frescobaldi years rest on Wikipedia and Decanter, the Napa adviser, the blue clay and Masseto's 1986 and 1987 on Decanter and FINE+RARE.
The adviser, André Tchelistcheff, is now named with his dates, 1901 to 1994: the refuter found them in the Wein.plus glossary, beside the author's Wikipedia and Wine History Project.

Decanter dates Mondavi's first share to 2000 and Wikipedia to November 1999, so the story says from 1999; the uncle by marriage rests on Wikipedia (the founder of Sassicaia's nephew was the founder's brother) and Decanter (both men married della Gherardesca daughters).
The Vendemmia d'Artista labels, every vintage since the 2006 by the estate's own page, are left out for want of a source slot.
The library's w-ornellaia-wine says the estate is now owned by Frescobaldi; the record tells the purchase of 2005 as history instead.
Living, kept out: the founder (Lodovico Antinori, in people.json) and Ferdinando Frescobaldi and Giovanni Geddes da Filicaja, met in the search, who should join people.json.

changed: story: the adviser was described as a Russian born veteran of the Napa Valley; now named, André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), with the Wein.plus glossary for his dates beside the author's two, and the report line rewritten.

story and cards: the Merlot of 1986 was "sold as Merlot dell'Ornellaia"; now "bottled as", since FINE+RARE and Vinfolio call it an experiment never released and most accounts make 1987 the first Masseto sold.

wine.making: "stainless steel and concrete tanks" now "stainless steel and, in later vintages, concrete tanks", since the sheets of 2010 and 2015 give steel alone and those of 2016 and 2020 steel and concrete.
open: The partnership years differ: Mondavi in from November 1999 or 2000, equal partners with the Frescobaldi in 2002, or the founder's last half sold to the Frescobaldi in 2003 by one account; the story's "from 1999" and "soon beside it" hold for all of them, and 2005 is in every account.

wine.name: Bolgheri Superiore Grattamacco
wine.classification: Superiore under the Bolgheri DOC, a red aged two years or more, one in oak
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about two thirds, with Merlot and a smaller share of Sangiovese.
wine.sites: The estate's own hill between Castagneto Carducci and Bolgheri, facing the Tyrrhenian Sea at about 100 to 200 metres, above the estates of the plain, with the sea breeze across it.
wine.making: Hand picked, the grapes ferment with their own yeasts in open conical oak vats, the cap punched down by hand, with long macerations. Eighteen months in French barriques, from new to second use, and a year in bottle follow before release.
wine.glass: Cassis and blackberry with myrtle, sour cherry and a salty, savoury edge, the Sangiovese showing beneath the Cabernet; medium to full bodied, firm and fresh rather than plush.
wine.ageing: Taut for its first six to eight years, it opens in its second decade; from a strong vintage it keeps twenty years or more.
wine.serve: Decant a young bottle an hour or two before serving at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The Superiore rank of Bolgheri red: two years of ageing or more, counted from 1 January after the harvest, one of them in oak.
The estate on its hill above the coast, founded in 1977, and the name of its flagship red.

records.table: The second estate of Bolgheri, founded in 1977, Grattamacco grows its Bolgheri Superiore on a hill above the sea between Castagneto Carducci and Bolgheri: Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Sangiovese. It tastes savoury and firm rather than plush.
records.story: Grattamacco began in 1977, when its founder bought a farm on a hill between Castagneto Carducci and Bolgheri, facing the sea. After San Guido it was the second estate of Bolgheri to plant for fine wine, and the estate calls its red the second Super Tuscan of the zone. Its first commercial vintage, 1982, sold as a table wine, blended Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Sangiovese by the estate's account, three years before the first Ornellaia. In 1986 the house planted Vermentino in place of Trebbiano, by its own account the first in Bolgheri. Created in 1983 for white and rosé, the Bolgheri DOC took in red wine in 1994; Grattamacco's red is a Bolgheri Superiore under those rules, which allow Sangiovese up to half the blend. Most of its neighbours left Sangiovese out, as the consorzio notes, but Grattamacco kept a share of it, fermented with wild yeasts in open oak vats. In 2002 the estate passed into ColleMassari, a family group of Tuscan estates. Open Grattamacco to show that Bolgheri Superiore may hold Sangiovese, and to taste Bolgheri from the hills rather than the plain: tighter, saltier and more savoury than the reds below it.

others.name: Grattamacco Bolgheri Rosso
others.note: The estate's younger red under the Bolgheri DOC, released before the Superiore.

others.name: Grattamacco Bolgheri Vermentino
others.note: The white from Vermentino, planted by the house in 1986 in place of Trebbiano.

traps: Bolgheri DOC allows Sangiovese and Syrah up to half the blend, so Grattamacco's Sangiovese is within the rules and no sign of an IGT.
Grattamacco stands on a hill between Castagneto Carducci and Bolgheri, higher than the estates of the plain, which changes the style.

cards.front: Grattamacco: which grape sets its Bolgheri Superiore apart from most of its neighbours?
cards.back: Sangiovese, a smaller share beside Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

cards.front: In which year was Grattamacco founded, the second estate of Bolgheri after San Guido?

questions.q: Which method of fermentation does Grattamacco use for its Bolgheri Superiore?
opts: With wild yeasts in open conical oak vats
With cultured yeasts in closed steel tanks
In clay amphorae buried in the ground
By carbonic maceration in sealed vats
questions.exp: The house ferments spontaneously in open oak vats, punched down by hand, with long macerations; closed steel tanks and cultured yeasts are the opposite of its method.

questions.q: Grattamacco was the second estate of Bolgheri to plant for fine wine. Which was its first commercial vintage?
questions.exp: The estate began in 1977 and sold its first wine from the 1982 vintage; 1985 is the first Ornellaia and 1968 the first Sassicaia sold.

sources.title: Vino Joy: Grattamacco, 35 years in the making
Consorzio Tutela Vini Bolgheri DOC: Wines

report: Primary: the estate's pages on the ColleMassari site (1977, first wine 1982 of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Sangiovese, the second Super Tuscan of the area, Vermentino of 1986, the group from 2002, the open vats, eighteen months in barrique and a year in bottle, about 100 to 200 metres) and the consorzio's rules (Superiore two years, one in oak; Sangiovese and Syrah up to half; Sangiovese rare in the zone's blends), read through search summaries; Vino Joy and The Buyer confirm 1977, the second estate and 1982.

The Buyer says Sangiovese made the majority of the 1982 and Merlot joined only in 1995, which the estate's own page contradicts (Merlot in the first blend), so the story gives no shares for the early vintages.

Left out for want of a second source: the founder's origin in Lombardy (one account says Bergamo), the writer who inspired him, organic farming from the outset, and the year Grattamacco first carried Bolgheri Superiore (1995 in one account); the ColleMassari estate's place in Montecucco rests on The Buyer alone and is left out.
The library's style line and traps agree with what was found; its claim of 'among the better whites of the appellation' for the Vermentino is a judgement the record does not repeat.
Living, kept out and for people.json: the founder, Piermario Meletti Cavallari, and the buyer of 2002, Claudio Tipa.

changed: story: the 1982 blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Sangiovese is now "by the estate's account" and "sold as a table wine", since The Buyer gives a Sangiovese majority with Merlot only from 1995, and no DOC covered a red before 1994.

story: the Sangiovese limit of half was tied to the rules of 1994; now told as the Superiore rank's rule, since Wikipedia gives the older rules as up to seven tenths Sangiovese, the consorzio's code as it stands half.
open: The early blend's shares and the year Grattamacco first carried Bolgheri Superiore were not settled.

wine.name: Paleo Rosso
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the regional category the house chooses for its single variety wines
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc alone since the 2001 vintage; the earlier vintages were blends led by Cabernet Sauvignon.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards at Bolgheri: for the later vintages Casa Nuova, on clay with stones of sandstone, Vignone, over limestone rock, and Ulivino, planted between 1998 and 2016; the 2001 came from Contessine, planted in 1983, and Puntone.
wine.making: The skins stay with the wine for three to six weeks of fermentation and maceration, in concrete tanks in later vintages. Then come fourteen to twenty months, mostly in barriques, a large share or all of them new; conical wooden vats and a stoneware amphora have since joined them.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant leaf, bramble and red plum with graphite, tobacco and the wild herbs of the coast, the green lift of Cabernet Franc kept ripe; full bodied, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Ready from about six years, it is fuller at ten to fifteen, and the strong years run to twenty or more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, with an hour or so in a decanter for a young bottle; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: A wild herb of the Tuscan coast, by the house's account, which gave the wine its name.
Indicazione Geografica Tipica for the whole of Tuscany, the house's choice for its single variety reds from Bolgheri.

records.table: Le Macchiole's Paleo Rosso was a blend until the 2001 vintage made it Cabernet Franc alone from Bolgheri, labelled Toscana IGT by the house's choice. Look for bramble, graphite and coastal herbs, the tannin fine.
records.story: When the first rules of the Bolgheri DOC were written in 1983, for white and rosé, a young couple founded Le Macchiole there: Eugenio Campolmi, who died in 2002 aged forty, and his wife; the house dates its vineyards to that year. Paleo, named for a wild herb of the coast, was first made in 1989, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Sangiovese, and the blend later took in Cabernet Franc. In 1994 came Messorio, a Merlot alone, and Scrio, a Syrah alone. With the 2001 vintage Paleo itself became Cabernet Franc alone. After his death the next year his widow took the estate on, later with their sons, keeping each wine to a single variety and the Toscana IGT on the label. Paleo Rosso, Cabernet Franc from Bolgheri, teaches two lessons: that a wine may change its grapes and keep its name, so a vintage must be dated before it is described, and that a single variety from inside the Bolgheri zone may carry the IGT rather than the DOC.

others.name: Messorio
others.note: Merlot alone, first made in 1994, the house's other single variety red of Bolgheri.

others.name: Scrio
others.note: Syrah alone, a reminder that Bolgheri is not only Bordeaux grapes.

others.name: Bolgheri Rosso
others.note: The house's blended red under the Bolgheri DOC.

traps: Paleo Rosso began as a blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon and became Cabernet Franc alone only with the 2001 vintage.
Paleo Rosso, Messorio and Scrio are labelled Toscana IGT, not Bolgheri DOC, though all three grow inside Bolgheri.
Messorio is Le Macchiole's Merlot; Masseto is the Merlot of the clay hill that was first part of Ornellaia.

cards.front: Paleo Rosso: with which vintage did it become Cabernet Franc alone?
cards.back: 2001; before that it was a blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon, first made in 1989.

cards.front: Le Macchiole makes a single variety red of Merlot and one of Syrah. Name them.
cards.back: Messorio, the Merlot, and Scrio, the Syrah.

questions.q: A guest orders Paleo Rosso of the 2016 vintage. Which grape is in the glass?
questions.exp: Since the 2001 vintage Paleo Rosso has been Cabernet Franc alone; Cabernet Sauvignon with Sangiovese was the first blend of 1989, and Merlot alone is Messorio.

questions.q: Le Macchiole first made Paleo in 1989. What was the wine before the 2001 vintage?
opts: A blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon
A Merlot from a clay hill
questions.exp: The 1989 was Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Sangiovese, and Cabernet Franc joined the blend later; Merlot went to Messorio and Syrah to Scrio.

sources.title: Decanter: Rising star Campolmi dies at 40

report: Primary: the house's own pages (vineyards since 1983, the founding couple, Paleo first made in 1989 and Cabernet Franc alone from 2001, the herb of the name, the parcels and the making across the vintage sheets of 1995 to the newest, Messorio and Scrio first made in 1994, the 1989 blend of Cabernet Sauvignon with Sangiovese and the 2000 of Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc), read through search summaries; the founder's death at forty in 2002 rests on Decanter's report of it and a second guide that gives 14 July 2002, not listed because its address carries a writer's name.
The founder is named with the year of his death only: his birth year (1961 or 1962 by his age) was not found in two sources; the integrator may prefer a description.
The founding year: 1983 by the house and the library, but Vinous says the couple bought the property in 1982 and one account dates a first vineyard to 1975.

The library's p-le-macchiole says the house chose the IGT to bottle single varieties the appellation does not favour; the consorzio's rules as they stand allow Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc each up to the whole blend, so a pure Cabernet Franc could be Bolgheri DOC, and the IGT is the house's choice; the rules in force in 2001 were not checked, so the record says only that the house chooses the IGT.
The library calls Paleo Italy's benchmark for the variety, a judgement the record does not repeat; the soils of the parcels were not found and are left out.
Living, kept out: the founder's widow (Cinzia Merli, in people.json) and their sons, Elia and Mattia Campolmi, who should join people.json.

changed: wine.sites: the parcels of the later sheets now carry their soils from the house's vineyards page (Casa Nuova clay with sandstone stones, Vignone over limestone rock), and the 2001 is drawn from Contessine, planted in 1983, and Puntone, as its sheet gives.

wine.making: the maceration "about a month or more" now "three to six weeks" (25 days in 2018, 40 on the newest sheet); "in steel for the early vintages and in concrete from the late 2000s" now "in concrete tanks in later vintages", the steel and the date found on no sheet; the barrel time "sixteen to twenty months" now "fourteen to twenty" (fourteen in 2008); new oak "a large share" now "a large share or all" (all new in 2001, 2016 and 2018); the vats and "stoneware amphorae" now "a stoneware amphora", as the newest sheet gives.
story: Scrio dated with Messorio to 1994, as the house's pages and two trade accounts give.
traps: the IGT trap reworded, no change of fact.
open: A search summary gives the denomination of the 1995 and 1996 Paleo sheets as Bolgheri Rosso Superiore DOC, so the Toscana IGT may date only from the single variety; the record no longer says when the IGT began.

One account gives the Bolgheri Rosso rules before 2011 as Cabernet Sauvignon from a tenth to four fifths, which would have kept a pure Cabernet Franc out of the DOC in 2001; with one source, the house's reason for the IGT is not told.
Eugenio Campolmi is named with the year of his death alone (Decanter and Chateau Monty give 14 July 2002, aged forty); his birth year was not found.

records.place: Notri, Suvereto, in the Alta Maremma on the Tuscan coast

wine.name: Redigaffi
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, the regional category for Tuscany
wine.grapes: Merlot alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: Merlot on the estate's Notri hillside at Suvereto, in the Colline Metallifere south of Bolgheri: markedly clay soils with a good share of pebbles, densely planted and cordon trained.
wine.making: About ten days of fermentation in temperature controlled stainless steel are followed by some twenty five days more on the skins. The wine is aged for eighteen to twenty months in new French barriques, bottled in summer and rested several months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and blackberry with cocoa, liquorice and sweet tobacco, a touch of vanilla from the new barrels; full bodied and velvety, with ripe, dense tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and open within five or six years, it fills out by ten; a strong vintage keeps fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: A large Bordeaux glass, at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle is the better for an hour or so in a decanter.

label.means: Named, by the house's account, for a small stream that flows near the estate.
A category open to wine from anywhere in Tuscany, under which the house sells its Merlot from Suvereto.
The estate's name: one founder's given name and surname, reversed.

records.table: South of Bolgheri, on the Notri hillside at Suvereto, Tua Rita grows the Merlot for Redigaffi, first set apart in two barrels in 1994 and aged in new French oak. Plum, black cherry and cocoa, velvety in the mouth; give it an hour in a decanter.
records.story: Tua Rita takes its name from one of its two founders, her first name and surname reversed. In 1984 she and her partner bought land in the Notri hills at Suvereto, south of Bolgheri, in the Alta Maremma; by the house's account they came to live close to nature, and wine came later. Giusto di Notri, a blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon, was first made with the 1992 vintage. In 1994 the couple set two barriques of Merlot apart from the rest, and they became the first Redigaffi, named for a small stream near the property. The 2000 vintage of Redigaffi drew wide notice abroad and is told as the estate's breakthrough. After the founder's partner died in 2010, the next generation of the family took on its running. Remember Redigaffi as Merlot alone from clay at Suvereto, aged in new French barriques, and as a sign that the coast's fine wine runs south of Bolgheri into the Colline Metallifere.

questions.exp: The house ages Redigaffi eighteen to twenty months in new French barriques, the source of its touch of vanilla; large Slavonian casks belong to traditional Sangiovese, not to this Merlot.

questions.q: Tua Rita set two barriques of Merlot apart from the rest of its wine and made the first Redigaffi. In which vintage?
questions.exp: The first Redigaffi is the 1994; the estate was founded in 1984, Giusto di Notri began with the 1992, and 2000 is the vintage that drew notice abroad.

sources.title: Tua Rita: Redigaffi, Toscana Merlot IGT, technical sheet

report: The house is not in the library, so every fact rests on its own pages (founded 1984 at Notri by the two founders, the name reversed, Redigaffi first made in 1994 and named for the stream, the making and soil of the technical sheets, the partner's death in 2010) read through search summaries, with Suvereto Wine, Decanter and other secondary accounts in the same searches for 1984, 1992, the two barriques of 1994 and the year 2000.
The founder is Rita Tua, not Rita Tesi as a common memory has it; the house's page says the name reverses her first name and surname.
The partner who died in 2010 is described rather than named: his birth year was not found.

The 2000 vintage's fame rests on a critic's mark, which the record does not give; the story says only that it drew wide notice abroad and that the family dates the turn to that year, after a family interview.

Giusto di Notri's blend differs between accounts (Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, or with Merlot and Cabernet Franc), so the note names only the lead and Merlot; the DOCG of Suvereto and the estate's other reds are left out for want of a source read.
Living, kept out and for people.json: Rita Tua, Simena Bisti, Stefano Frascolla and Giovanni Frascolla.
